newsitem.title: USA: Merck sees strong profits, says will weather patent losses.
newsitem.headline: Merck sees strong profits, says will weather patent losses.

text.p: Merck & Co. Inc., predicting strong earnings, said Wednesday it expects the company's lineup of new drugs to more than offset patent expirations of key moneymakers coming at the end of the decade.
Merck said its current quarter and full-year 1997 earnings will be at the top of analysts' estimates, thanks to strong sales of several new products as well as older products.

Analysts expect Merck to earn the equivalent of $3.13 to $3.19 per share in 1996, which implies fourth-quarter earnings of 80 cents to 86 cents per share. Estimates for 1997 earnings are $3.55 to $3.75.

"Based on the strength of our recent performance and the momentum we've been building this year, we expect our fourth-quarter earnings to come in at the top of analysts' estimates," said Raymond Gilmartin, Merck's chairman and chief executive, told a meeting of securities analysts here.
"In the years beyond 1997, we believe we clearly have the elements in place to deliver on our long-standing objective of top-quartile earnings growth relative to other leading health-care companies."
Merck executives highlighted new drugs for which Merck plans to file for approval in the coming months and others further back in the drug development process.
"We are juggling a very large portfolio," said Edward Scolnick, president of Merck Research Laboratories.
He said the new drugs would allow the company to "clearly weather the storm of patent expirations at the end of the decade."

Merck faces the expirations of U.S. patents on key drugs, including its Vasotec high blood pressure and heart failure drug and Pepcid anti-ulcer treatment, in the year 2000. Its cholesterol-lowering agent Mevacor and the high blood pressure and heart failure drug Prinivil go off patent in the United States in 2001.
Loss of patent on widely used drugs typically opens the door to cut-price generic competitors. Analysts said Merck appeared to be positioning itself to absorb the blow.
"They clearly have a very good strategy for offsetting the generics," said James Keeney of Rodman and Renshaw.

Backing the new drugs and those already on the market, including the osteoporosis drug Fosamax and the AIDS treatment Crixivan, Merck said it was boosting its research and development spending in 1997 to $1.7 billion, a 16 percent rise over 1996 levels. Executives said the company was adding 600 U.S. sales representatives to its current force of 2,500.
Scolnick said Merck plans to file for approval of its Propecia drug for treating male pattern hair loss with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration later this month.

He displayed before-and-after photographs showing that men in a clinical trial had regrown hair using the drug, a pill that is a lower-dose version of a Merck drug for treating enlarged prostates. "Propecia really works and is well-tolerated," he said.
Propecia will go up against Pharmacia & Upjohn Inc.'s Rogaine, which is a topical solution sold without a prescription.
Skolnick said Merck planned to file for FDA marketing approval of a new asthma pill, Singulair, in 1997's first quarter.
Merck's stock rose 75 cents to $77 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading.
